title: Diversity in the Living World
description: Grade 6 Science: the variety of plants and animals, how we group and classify organisms, and habitats with their living and non-living parts. Notes, examples and a test.

topics.title: The Variety of Plants and Animals
topics.concept:
Look around and you will find an amazing variety of living things — tall trees and tiny mosses, soaring eagles and crawling ants, fish in water and camels in the desert. This huge variety of living organisms is called biodiversity.

Even within one group, living things differ from one another. Plants, for example, come in different forms:

  • Herbs — small plants with soft, green stems (mint, coriander, grass).
  • Shrubs — medium, bushy plants with woody stems branching near the ground (rose, hibiscus).
  • Trees — tall, big plants with a thick, woody main stem called a trunk (mango, neem).
  • Climbers and creepers — plants with weak stems; climbers rise with support, creepers spread along the ground (money plant; pumpkin).

Animals also vary in where they live, what they eat and how they move. Some live on land, some in water, some can fly. Based on food, animals may be herbivores (plant-eaters, like cows), carnivores (meat-eaters, like lions) or omnivores (eat both, like humans and bears). This rich variety is found everywhere — even a small garden is home to dozens of different living things.

examples.problem: Example 1: Classify these plants as herb, shrub or tree: mint, rose, mango.
examples.solution:
Sort by size and the type of stem.

  • Mint — small, soft stem → herb.
  • Rose — bushy, woody near the ground → shrub.
  • Mango — tall, thick trunk → tree.
examples.answer: Mint is a herb, rose is a shrub, and mango is a tree.

examples.problem: Example 2: A cow eats only grass and plants. What is such an animal called?
examples.solution:
Group animals by what they eat.

  • An animal that eats only plants is a herbivore.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the name for the great variety of living things found on Earth?
examples.solution:
There is a special word for the variety of life.

  • The variety of living organisms is called biodiversity.

recap:
• The huge variety of living organisms is called biodiversity.
  • Plants include herbs, shrubs, trees, climbers and creepers, differing in size and stem.
  • By food, animals are herbivores, carnivores or omnivores.
  • Living things vary in where they live, what they eat and how they move.

quiz.q: A tall plant with a thick, woody trunk is a:
quiz.explanation: Trees are big plants with a thick woody trunk.

quiz.q: An animal that eats both plants and other animals is called a/an:
quiz.explanation: Omnivores eat both plants and animals.

topics.title: Grouping and Classification of Organisms
topics.concept:
Because there are millions of kinds of living things, scientists group them to study them more easily. Putting organisms with similar features together is called classification. We classify by looking at shared characteristics — such as where an organism lives, how it moves, what its body is like, or how it gets food.

A first, simple division is into plants and animals:

  • Plants — usually green, fixed in one place, make their own food, and grow throughout life.
  • Animals — can usually move from place to place, cannot make their own food (they eat plants or other animals), and most stop growing after a certain stage.

Animals can be grouped further. A useful grouping is by whether they have a backbone:

  • Vertebrates — animals that have a backbone (fish, frogs, snakes, birds, cats, humans).
  • Invertebrates — animals without a backbone (ants, worms, spiders, snails, jellyfish).

Classification is helpful because it lets us see how living things are similar and different, makes them easier to identify and study, and shows how life on Earth is connected.

examples.problem: Example 1: Give one important difference between most plants and most animals.
examples.solution:
Compare a key feature.

  • Most plants make their own food and stay fixed in one place.
  • Most animals cannot make their own food and can move about.
examples.answer: Plants make their own food and are fixed in place, while animals cannot make their own food and can usually move.

examples.problem: Example 2: Classify as vertebrate or invertebrate: frog, ant, fish, earthworm.
examples.solution:
Check for a backbone.

  • Frog and fish have a backbone → vertebrates.
  • Ant and earthworm have no backbone → invertebrates.
examples.answer: Frog and fish are vertebrates; ant and earthworm are invertebrates.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why do scientists classify living things?
examples.solution:
Classification organises a huge variety of organisms.

  • It makes them easier to identify and study.
  • It shows how organisms are similar, different and connected.
examples.answer: To organise the huge variety of life so it is easier to identify, study and understand the links between organisms.

recap:
• Classification = grouping organisms by shared characteristics.
  • A first split is plants (make food, fixed) vs animals (eat food, can move).
  • Animals can be vertebrates (with backbone) or invertebrates (without backbone).
  • Classification helps us identify, study and connect living things.

quiz.q: Animals that have a backbone are called:
quiz.explanation: Vertebrates are animals with a backbone.

quiz.q: Which of these is an invertebrate?
quiz.explanation: An ant has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate.

topics.title: Habitats and Environmental Interactions
topics.concept:
The place where a plant or animal naturally lives is called its habitat. A habitat provides an organism with everything it needs — food, water, air, shelter and a place to reproduce. A forest, a pond, a desert and the sea are all habitats.

Habitats are of two broad kinds:

  • Terrestrial habitats — on land (forests, grasslands, deserts, mountains).
  • Aquatic habitats — in water (ponds, rivers, lakes, oceans).

Every habitat has two kinds of parts. The living (biotic) parts are the plants, animals and other organisms. The non-living (abiotic) parts are things like sunlight, water, air, soil and temperature. The living and non-living parts constantly affect one another — this is an environmental interaction. For instance, the amount of water and sunlight (non-living) decides which plants can grow, and those plants (living) provide food and shelter for animals.

Organisms have special features, called adaptations, that suit them to their habitat. A fish has gills and fins to live in water; a camel has long legs and stores fat in its hump to survive the hot desert; a cactus stores water in its thick stem. An organism removed from its habitat may not survive, which is why protecting habitats is so important.

examples.problem: Example 1: A pond is a habitat. Give one living and one non-living part of it.
examples.solution:
Habitats have biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) parts.

  • Living part: fish (or water plants, frogs).
  • Non-living part: water (or sunlight, air).
examples.answer: Living part: a fish; non-living part: the water (other answers such as plants/sunlight are also correct).

examples.problem: Example 2: How is a camel adapted to live in the hot, dry desert?
examples.solution:
Adaptations suit an organism to its habitat.

  • It stores fat in its hump to last without food.
  • Long legs keep its body away from the hot sand and it can go long without water.
examples.answer: It stores fat in its hump, has long legs to stay above the hot sand and can survive a long time without water.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why might a fish die if taken out of its watery habitat?
examples.solution:
An organism depends on its habitat to meet its needs.

  • A fish breathes using gills, which work only in water.
  • Out of water it cannot get oxygen, so it cannot survive.
examples.answer: A fish breathes through gills that work only in water, so out of its habitat it cannot get oxygen and dies.

recap:
• A habitat is the natural home of an organism, giving it food, water, air and shelter.
  • Habitats are terrestrial (land) or aquatic (water).
  • Each habitat has living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts that interact.
  • Adaptations are special features that suit an organism to its habitat.

quiz.q: The natural home of a plant or animal is called its:
quiz.explanation: A habitat is the place where an organism naturally lives.

quiz.q: Sunlight, water and air in a habitat are examples of its ___ parts.
quiz.explanation: Sunlight, water and air are non-living (abiotic) parts of a habitat.

questions.q: The huge variety of living organisms on Earth is called:
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms.

questions.q: Small plants with soft green stems are called:
questions.explanation: Herbs are small plants with soft, green stems.

questions.q: A bushy plant with woody stems branching near the ground is a:
questions.explanation: Shrubs are medium, bushy plants with woody stems near the ground.

questions.q: An animal that eats only plants is a:
questions.explanation: Herbivores eat only plants.

questions.q: Putting organisms with similar features into groups is called:
questions.explanation: Grouping organisms by shared features is classification.

questions.q: Which feature do most plants have but most animals do not?
questions.explanation: Most plants make their own food; animals cannot.

questions.q: Animals that have a backbone are called:
questions.explanation: Vertebrates have a backbone.

questions.q: Which of these is an invertebrate?
questions.explanation: An earthworm has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate.

questions.q: The natural home of an organism is its:
questions.explanation: A habitat is where an organism naturally lives.

questions.q: A pond and a river are examples of ___ habitats.
questions.explanation: Water habitats are aquatic habitats.

questions.q: The living parts of a habitat are called its:
questions.explanation: Living parts of a habitat are the biotic parts.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-living (abiotic) part of a habitat?
questions.explanation: Sunlight is a non-living (abiotic) part of a habitat.

questions.q: A special feature that helps an organism survive in its habitat is called a/an:
questions.explanation: An adaptation suits an organism to its habitat.

questions.q: A fish can live in water because it has gills and:
questions.explanation: Gills let a fish breathe in water and fins help it swim.

questions.q: Why is it important to protect habitats?
options: Organisms depend on their habitat to survive
questions.explanation: Organisms need their habitat for food, shelter and survival, so habitats must be protected.

questions.q: A whale lives in the sea but, unlike a fish, comes up to breathe air. This shows that animals living in the same habitat can still:
questions.explanation: Whales breathe air with lungs while fish use gills; the same habitat can hold different adaptations.

questions.q: Why does a cactus have a thick stem and spiny (reduced) leaves?
options: To store water and lose less of it in the desert
questions.explanation: The thick stem stores water and spines reduce water loss, suiting the dry desert.

questions.q: A spider, a snail and a jellyfish belong to the same broad group because they all:
questions.explanation: All three are invertebrates — they have no backbone.

questions.q: In a forest, the plants depend on sunlight and rain, and animals depend on plants for food. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: It shows environmental interaction between the biotic and abiotic parts of a habitat.

questions.q: Which list correctly goes from SMALLEST to LARGEST plant type?
questions.explanation: Herbs are smallest, shrubs medium and trees largest.

questions.q: Classifying first into 'plants' and 'animals', then animals into 'vertebrates' and 'invertebrates', shows that classification can be done in:
options: Steps, from broad groups to smaller groups
questions.explanation: Classification moves step by step from broad groups to smaller, more specific groups.
